transcript:
Meeting Header:
Date: 2026-12-28
Start: 15:00 PST
Duration: ~58 minutes
Attendees: Ethan Chen (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Mark Reynolds (Zenfolio Head of ML), Lisa Gomez (Zenfolio Infra), Tom Becker (Zenfolio Product)

Summary:
Quick POC scoping to align on success criteria, what traces & token histograms Zenfolio can share, target QPS/concurrency, and timeline for a 2-week pilot. Discussed latency SLOs, cost targets, Dedicated vs Hosted, security checkpoints (SOC2, KMS), and concrete next steps.

Topics:
- Traffic modeling: QPS, concurrency, peak vs avg
- Token distribution: prompt/input lengths, expected completion lengths
- Benchmarks: baseline metrics, scripted workloads, cold vs warm cache
- Top success criteria: P95 latency, cost per 1M tokens, stability under 99th percentile traffic
- Timeline: data share -> baseline -> pilot -> results

Transcript:
[00:00] Ethan Chen: Hey everyone, um thanks for joining. Um this is Ethan from Redwood, AE on the account, and Priya our SE is with me. Mark, Lisa, Tom, good to see you.
[00:12] Mark Reynolds: Hey, yeah thanks. We've been looking at inference providers, you know, OpenAI for a lot of the quick experiments but we need more control for production. We're especially focused on latency and cost per message for the payments reconciliation flows.
[00:26] Priya Nair: Cool, can you give us a quick sense of current traffic shape - average QPS, burst, payload sizes? Even ballparks help us size a Dedicated pool or guide hosted config.
[00:36] Tom Becker: Sure. So avg qps is kinda tricky, we see about 5 QPS steady state during business hours, spikes up to 80 QPS in peak batch windows. Typical requests are single-turn prompts for reconciliation - inputs around 120 tokens, outputs typically 30-70 tokens. For some long-form investigative queries, we're seeing outputs up to 400 tokens, but those are <1% of calls.
[01:05] Lisa Gomez: To add, concurrency we measure at the app level - we see bursts with about 40 concurrent in-flight inference calls during peak batch runs. We're not currently doing explicit batching in the app side.
[01:18] Ethan Chen: Great, that helps. So for modeling, we usually ask for percentile token histograms and a 48h trace if possible. You mentioned bursts to 80 QPS and 40 concurrency - that's useful. Our rough math: with inputs 120 + outputs 70 on average that's 190 tokens per request, at 80 QPS that's ~15k tokens/s, which maps to X GPU throughput depending on model/quantization.
[01:46] Mark Reynolds: When you say X GPU throughput, can you give a concrete example? Like if we pick a 13B model, what would that look like in Dedicated vs hosted?
[01:54] Priya Nair: Yeah, roughly - a modern 13B quantized model on an A100-class instance in our Dedicated fleet can handle continuous throughput around Y tokens/sec with good batching, but latency SLOs change if you force low p95. For low latency (p95 < 500ms) for single requests you'd need either more replica capacity or smaller models / better batching + caching. We'll run concrete numbers in the benchmark.
[02:18] Tom Becker: Our target P95 is sub 800ms for normal reconciliation calls and sub 1.2s for the occasional long investigative queries. Cost target is roughly $0.50 per 1k completed prompts - I know that's fuzzy.
[02:33] Ethan Chen: That's super helpful. We'll try to map to cost per 1M tokens in the benchmark. For the pilot, success criteria we typically see enterprise customers set: 1) functional correctness against sample prompt set, 2) P95 latency under target (you said 800ms), 3) stable throughput across burst windows, and 4) unit cost within your budget. Anything else to add?
[02:52] Mark Reynolds: Auditability - we need audit logs for every inference and encryption with KMS. Also SSO and RBAC for the console access.
[03:01] Priya Nair: Yep that's standard, we have SOC2 and we can provide our security pack. For Private deployments we can integrate with customer KMS and on-prem if needed. Lisa, are you okay to share network constraints? VPC peering, allowlist windows?
[03:14] Lisa Gomez: We'll need VPC peering for Dedicated, and an allowlist window. Also want to understand how you handle KV caching and session tokens - we can't leak payment tokens into shared cache.
[03:25] Ethan Chen: Absolutely - we support per-tenant KV cache and optional cache bypass. We'll document that. For the POC we'll propose a baseline on Hosted with trace replay, then a Dedicated baseline if you prefer. Timeline-wise we can start once you share traces - 2-3 days to configure harness, then 48h baseline run, analyze, then another 1 week for tuning and a final run.

[03:52] Mark Reynolds: Sounds reasonable. For the traces, what format is easiest?
[03:56] Priya Nair: CSV or NDJSON with fields: timestamp, prompt_tokens, completion_tokens, model_hint, request_id. Histogram for token lengths is fine too.
[04:06] Tom Becker: We'll export out 48 hours by EOD tomorrow.

[04:10] Ethan Chen: Perfect. On traffic modeling - we look at average QPS, peak QPS, and burst length. Also the concurrency distribution. For example your peak 80 QPS with 40 concurrency suggests average in-flight latency of 0.5-2.0s which aligns with your P95 target.
[04:28] Priya Nair: When we run the benchmark, we'll create four synthetic workload patterns: steady-state low-latency (5 QPS), traffic spiky bursts (simulate 80 QPS for 5-10 minutes), mixed profile with 1% long completions (400 tokens), and cache-warm vs cold runs. We'll report p50/p95/p99 latencies and token/sec throughput.
[04:51] Lisa Gomez: One other constraint - we have PCI compliance so logs with cardholder data must be redacted before sharing. We only can share token-length histograms and prompts with PHI removed.
[05:01] Ethan Chen: Understood. We'll provide a scrub script and handling guidelines. For cost modeling we also want to know your model choice - are you considering larger models than 13B? Open to Llama-2-70B type? That will change GPU needs significantly.
[05:16] Mark Reynolds: For reconciliation 13B is probably fine; for investigative queries maybe 33B but we can start with 13B for the pilot.

[05:24] Tom Becker: Curious about KV cache - can Redwood do prefix caching to reduce repeated token generation across similar prompts? We have a lot of templated prompts.
[05:33] Priya Nair: Yes, automatic prefix/KV caching is supported - in Dedicated or Private we can enable per-tenant cache. That typically reduces token work for templated prompts a lot. We'll include cache-on and cache-off runs in the benchmark.

[05:48] Ethan Chen: OK action recap: Priya will share benchmark harness and runbook, Ethan will send pricing and SOW, Mark will provide traces and token histogram, Lisa will confirm network details. We'll aim for baseline next week and pilot the week after.

[06:00] Mark Reynolds: One operational question - what telemetry do we get in the console? We need token-level cost breakdown, per-route latency, and model-level tracing.
[06:10] Priya Nair: Redwood Console gives per-route token and latency breakdown, we can also add tracing hooks and custom tags. We'll show a demo in the follow-up if helpful.
[06:22] Tom Becker: Are there any hidden costs we should be aware of with Dedicated - like network egress or licensing fees?
[06:28] Ethan Chen: Standard cloud egress applies, but we'll include estimated egress based on your trace. No hidden runtime licensing; Dedicated is reserved capacity commit plus usage for overage. We'll detail in the SOW.

[06:40] Lisa Gomez: For security review: we need SOC2 report, ISO, and an offer to do a short on-call contact for incident window during the POC.
[06:49] Ethan Chen: We can provide SOC2 and customer-specific incident contact. We'll include support hours in the pilot SOW.

[07:00] Priya Nair: For the benchmark specifics, please confirm the target model (13B quantized) and whether we should enable half-precision or int8 quantization. That affects throughput numbers.
[07:12] Mark Reynolds: Let's start with the quantized 13B int8 profile.

[07:16] Tom Becker: Timeline check - you said 2-3 days to configure harness. Can we lock dates? We're on a year-end freeze Jan 1-3, so earlier is better.
[07:26] Ethan Chen: If you can send traces by Jan 4, we can configure Jan 5-6, run baseline Jan 7-8, and tuning Jan 11-14, results by Jan 15. That fits a 2-week window but shifted a little due to holidays.
[07:43] Mark Reynolds: Works for us. One more thing on success criteria - we want to verify correctness against a labeled test set of 120 prompts. We'll need a pass/fail threshold on outputs.
[07:55] Priya Nair: We can run evaluation harness against that labeled set and report quality metrics. If quality regresses vs your accuracy threshold we can test model variants or parameter tweaks.

[08:10] Ethan Chen: Great - recap of next steps and owners again.
[08:14] Priya Nair: I'll put the runbook link in the follow-up and include example scripts for generating the workload (wrk-style harness) and parsing token histograms.
[08:25] Tom Becker: We'll also need a proof of no-PHI leakage in the logs; appreciate the scrub script.

[08:32] Ethan Chen: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with an email with links: pricing/SOW draft, benchmark harness link, security pack, and schedule invite for the baseline run.
[08:44] Mark Reynolds: Thanks, appreciate the detail.
[08:46] Lisa Gomez: Thanks.
[08:48] (call ends)
